29 What is a possible charge on a particle?
A
6.40 × 10–20
C
B
4.00 × 10–19
C
C
1.12 × 10–18
C
D
9.11 × 10–18
C

hints: Notice the four values are all around $10^{-19} \text{ C}$ to $10^{-18} \text{ C}$ - think what smallest unit of free charge sets the scale.
Recall charge is quantised as $Q = n e$ where $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and $n$ must be an integer for an isolated particle.
Test each value by calculating $Q/e$ and look for the one that gives a whole number with no remainder.
walkthrough: Identify the rule: any isolated particle must carry a charge that is an integer multiple of the elementary charge, $Q = n e$.
State the elementary charge $e = 1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ and that $n = Q/e$ must be $1, 2, 3...$.
Check the values: for $1.12 \times 10^{-18} \text{ C}$, calculate $n = (1.12 \times 10^{-18})/(1.60 \times 10^{-19})$.
Simplify: $1.12/0.160 = 7.0$, so $Q = 7e$, which satisfies quantisation with integer $n = 7$.
The other values give $0.4$, $2.5$ and about $56.9$, which are non-integers and so are not allowed. This is option C.

A.explanation: Dividing $6.40 \times 10^{-20} \text{ C}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives $0.4$, which is not a whole number of elementary charges.

B.explanation: Dividing $4.00 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives $2.5$, which is not a whole number of elementary charges.

C.explanation: Dividing $1.12 \times 10^{-18} \text{ C}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives $7$, an integer number of elementary charges.

D.explanation: Dividing $9.11 \times 10^{-18} \text{ C}$ by $1.60 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$ gives about $57$, not an exact integer, so it cannot be a quantised charge.
